newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Anglo upbeat on deep level gold recovery.
newsitem.headline: Anglo upbeat on deep level gold recovery.

text.p: Anglo American Corp of South Africa said on Friday it was confident that its home country's remaining gold resources could be mined profitably despite much of the metal lying kilometres below the earth's surface.

Ian Cockerill, technical director of the mining giant's gold arm Anglogold, said the estimated 20,000 tonnes of gold deposits left in the ground could be brought to account through effective people management and appropriate proven technologies.

"Some 46,000 tonnes have been recovered from the (Witwatersrand) basin in the past 110 years but by our estimate there remain resources of some 20,000 tonnes still to be mined," Cockerill told the African Mining Conference in Cape Town.
He said Anglo's five gold producing mines, Vaal Reefs, Western Deep Levels , Freegold, Elandsrand and Ergo, had remaining reserves conservatively estimated at 4,100 tonnes.
"Added to this is the prospect of an additional 1,500 tonnes at down to 5,000 metres in the Western Ultra Deep Levels lease adjacent to Western Deep Levels."

He said Anglo believed it had the capacity to develop single lift shafts -- as opposed to previous three shaft structures which were costly and took a long to construct -- down to 4,000 metres which could lift economic payloads from these depths.
"Developing a single sub-shaft another 1,000 metres to 5,000 metres does not pose a problem," he said.
Advances in the development of more sophisticated stoping methodology and seismic monitoring would further help to unearth deep gold riches.

"Sequential grid mining was successfully pioneered in the Anglogold group at Elandsrand and is now being introduced at some of the other group operations, for example, at Western Deep Levels and Vaal Reefs No 11 shaft," Cockerill said.
Improved labour productivity on the back of workplace re-engineering programmes at Elandsrand also pointed to a better and cheaper rate of recovery of gold and an easing of pressure on margins.
Margins in the gold mining industry had reached an all-time low of 18.6 percent in 1995, he said.
"The sun is far from setting on South African gold mining; it has just popped over the horizon, appropriately at the dawn of a new golden century," Cockerill said.
